flashcard_questions.q: What does paper stand for as an extended metaphor in Tissue?
flashcard_questions.a: The fragility of human life and of the structures we build to control it.

flashcard_questions.q: Which opening line of Tissue states that change is possible?
flashcard_questions.a: “Paper that lets the light shine through, this is what could alter things.”

flashcard_questions.q: What does Dharker say we would notice “if buildings were paper”?
flashcard_questions.a: We would “feel their drift, see how easily they fall away on a sigh”.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the blunt sentence “Maps too” argue about national borders?
flashcard_questions.a: They are human inventions drawn on paper, not natural laws.

flashcard_questions.q: Which simile compares shop receipts to something the wind can carry?
flashcard_questions.a: They “might fly our lives like paper kites”.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Dharker criticise through “capitals and monoliths”?
flashcard_questions.a: Human pride, which builds permanent structures that matter less than human life.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the word ‘tissue’ come to mean in the final stanzas?
Which single line forms the last stanza of Tissue?
What does the short-stanza form of Tissue mirror?
flashcard_questions.a: Thin layers of paper — the form imitates the content.

flashcard_questions.q: Which day of remembrance is Poppies set around?
Which dressmaking metaphor conveys the mother's anxiety in Poppies?
flashcard_questions.a: Her stomach “busy making tucks, darts, pleats”.

flashcard_questions.q: Which simile shows the son's excitement about leaving home?
flashcard_questions.a: “The world overflowing like a treasure chest”

flashcard_questions.q: Which metaphor presents the son's departure as a release?
flashcard_questions.a: She “released a song bird from its cage”.

flashcard_questions.q: Which word carries childhood innocence into the war memorial scene?
What does the verb ‘bandaged’ link in “Sellotape bandaged around my hand”?
flashcard_questions.a: A domestic object to injury and to war.

notes: 15 cards: 7 quotation-to-technique or effect, 5 theme-to-quotation, 2 structure and form (the layered stanzas, the one-line final stanza), 1 context card (Armistice Sunday). Reworded the extended-metaphor and light-symbol answers so neither reads as a three-item list. Dropped the poets' biographies and the closing comparison paragraph — the comparison sets up an essay, not a card with one right answer.
